ESTABLISHING CREDIBLE COP31 LEADERSHIP

Co-hosting the 31st UN Climate Change Conference of Parties (COP31) presents Türkiye and Australia with a significant opportunity to demonstrate credible climate leadership and shape a lasting global legacy. As incoming COP Presidents, both countries can exert substantial influence over the ambition, momentum, and diplomatic outcomes of the negotiations. Their ability to drive progress, broker agreements, and maintain political trust will define whether COP31 delivers meaningful results. Yet none of this is possible without a strong foundation of integrity.

Integrity must be embedded from the earliest preparations through to the closing plenary, including in fundamental organisational decisions about participation, access, and influence. In this regard, Türkiye’s role at COP31 in Antalya will be particularly significant. As host, Türkiye will assume primary operational and logistical
responsibilities for the conference, including construction, infrastructure, and contracting, areas where transparency and safeguards against corruption are critical1.

Australia’s role as President of the Negotiations will be equally critical. Australian leadership will be responsible for convening consultations and meetings throughout the year to inform the negotiations, steering discussions during COP31, preparing and presenting draft decision texts, and ultimately facilitating consensus among Parties. This role carries clear responsibility to prevent negotiations from being dominated by powerful states or industry interests at the expense of the most climate vulnerable groups, and to ensure the inclusiveness of the process.

The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) currently lacks formal safeguards to protect the integrity of COP Presidencies. There are no clear, system wide definitions of conflicts of interest, nor binding rules for identifying, managing, or mitigating them2. COP Presidency teams are designated by host country governments and are not subject to UN-level vetting, eligibility criteria, or integrity screening. In this context, delivering a credible COP31 requires the co-hosts to take proactive steps to demonstrate their commitments to uphold the integrity and fairness of the negotiation process, ensure inclusive and transparent engagement, and shield the conference from undue influence.

In his letter of 13 April 2026, COP31 President Designate Murat Kurum committed to conducting the process in Antalya in a transparent, predictable, and inclusive manner, grounded in dialogue, consensus, and action3. To realise these commitments in practice, Transparency International is calling on the Turkish and Australian leadership of COP31 to adopt voluntary integrity measures ahead of the conference.

The COP31 Presidency should issue a joint public commitment to voluntary integrity measures that enhance transparency, strengthen accountability, and support the delivery of an effective and credible COP. These should include transparency on Presidency interests and decision‑making, safeguards to prevent and manage conflicts of interest, independent oversight mechanisms, and disclosure of lobbying activities, advisory roles, and contracts issued by the hosts for COP organisation, particularly those linked to high‑polluting industries.

Communicated together by Türkiye and Australia, such a declaration would reinforce international trust, elevate both countries’ diplomatic standing, and set a positive precedent for future Presidencies.
WHY INTEGRITY MATTERS FOR COP PRESIDENCY
TRANSPARENCY IN COP ORGANISATION

In climate diplomacy, process is just as important as substance. How a COP is organised directly shapes trust in the Presidency and, ultimately, the willingness of Parties to reach agreement. When a Presidency appears biased or closely aligned with polluting interests seeking to slow progress, trust erodes. Parties become defensive, observers disengage, and the likelihood of weak, or failed outcomes increase.
These risks are not theoretical. Recent COPs show how weaknesses in organisation, access and contracting can quickly undermine trust in a Presidency.
At COP26 in Glasgow, civil society groups, particularly from the Global South, reported “unprecedented”

• restriction on access to negotiations4. High travel and accommodation costs, visa-related hurdles and Covid-19 travel rules, including bans on red-listed countries5, significantly limited the participation of thousands of representatives from frontline communities, undermining perceptions of inclusiveness and the legitimacy of outcomes.

• At COP29 in Baku, the Presidency faced criticism over potential conflicts of interest, including links to Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR and sponsorship arrangements tied to the family of the President of Azerbaijan6. These concerns raised questions about rent-seeking and the independency of decision-making.
In the leadup to COP30 in Belém, civil society raised concerns about a media contract to Edelman, public

• relations firm with links to fossil fuel companies, such as Shell. The contract involved assisting the Brazilian Presidency to “craft a strategic narrative” for COP30, which prompted questions about conflicts of interest7.

In response to emerging concerns, the Brazilian Presidency voluntarily implemented a set of integrity measures ahead of COP30. These included the establishment of a Transparency Portal, through which official information on conference-related expenditures, contracts, organisational structures, and administrative procedures was made publicly accessible, as well as the publication of public engagement schedules for the COP30 Presidency team8. In addition, Brazil established a dedicated COP30 Ombudsman to receive reports, complaints, or suggestions during the conference9. It also organised the first Global Ethical Stocktake, aimed at bringing together civil society contributions to COP30 to help accelerate the implementation of the Paris Agreement10.

While these measures did not address all integrity risks inherent in the COP process11, they nonetheless represented an incremental and constructive step towards greater transparency, public scrutiny, and accountability.

COP31 presents an opportunity to learn and build from these experiences to reach best practices. Türkiye and Australia should seize this momentum. Together, they should ensure that the conference, including the pre-COP, which Australia is co-organising in partnership with Pacific Island countries, is planned and delivered through transparent procurement and contracting processes, robust conflict of interest safeguards for both Presidency teams, and firm measures to prevent corruption, corporate capture, rent seeking, or risky sponsorship by highly polluting industries. A clean and transparent Presidency is as much a matter of good governance as it is essential to delivering a credible and successful climate negotiations.

Türkiye and Australia must lead by example. A Presidency that calls for transparency and ambition must visibly and consistently demonstrate both at every stage of the process, positioning Türkiye and Australia as standard setters for integrity in global climate diplomacy.
PRESIDENCY LEADERSHIP AND INTEGRITY IN CLIMATE NEGOTIATIONS
Beyond organisation, integrity is equally critical in how the Presidency steers the negotiations themselves. Recent COPs demonstrate the stakes.
At COP28 in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) Presidency, led by Sultan Al Jaber while he

• simultaneously served as CEO of the national oil company ADNOC, faced intense pressure from oil‑producing states opposed to fossil fuel phase-out12. Early Global Stocktake drafts prepared by the Presidency were widely criticised as insufficiently ambitious by more than 100 Parties13, prompting concerns about the influence of fossil fuel interests. Although references to fossil fuels were ultimately included, this episode illustrates how quickly trust can erode and jeopardise negotiated outcomes.
In contrast, Brazil emphasised Indigenous leadership and representation at COP30 in Belém, framing the

• conference as a mutirão, a concept rooted in Indigenous traditions of collective effort14. As a result, COP30 hosted the largest Indigenous delegation in the history of the UNFCCC15. However, access to negotiation rooms and final drafting processes remained limited16, demonstrating that presence alone does not guarantee meaningful participation in climate decision-making.

Ahead of Parties convening in Antalya in November 2026, Fiji will host the COP31 pre-COP meeting, with a special leaders’ component in Tuvalu. Through its partnership role, Australia has an extraordinary opportunity to ensure Pacific priorities and voices are placed at the centre of COP31. The pre-COP meetings aim to direct diplomatic attention to climate-vulnerable nations and frontline climate impacts and ensure that regional priorities meaningfully inform the COP31 agenda17. If delivered credibly and inclusively, such efforts can enhance the legitimacy of the process and contribute to more constructive and ambitious outcomes.

The importance of integrity and leadership by climate vulnerable states was underscored in April 2026, when Pacific leaders collectively called for stronger UNFCCC safeguards through the Tassiriki Call for a Fossil Fuel Free Pacific, including measures to protect global climate governance from undue influence and to advance clear conflict-of-interest and transparency rules18.

As President of the Negotiations, Australia will need to balance competing priorities, ensure that smaller and less‑ resourced delegations are not sidelined, and resist pressure from actors seeking to delay or weaken climate action. Achieving this requires diplomatic skill, a strong command of UNFCCC processes, and a clear commitment to fairness and integrity. Parties and observer groups will be watching closely how Australia navigates the tension between its global climate leadership ambitions and its ongoing role as one of the world’s largest fossil fuel producers, exporters, and subsidisers19,20. Concrete safeguards ensuring that polluting interests have no influence over the Presidency team or negotiation outcomes will be essential to Australia’s credibility in this role.
RECOMMENDATIONS

Transparency International is calling on the COP31 Presidency to publicly commit the following voluntary integrity measures and apply them across all processes related to COP31, including the pre-COP in Fiji:
Transparency in decision-making and affiliations
Publish a declaration of interests for all members of the COP Presidency team and negotiators, disclosing
• any financial, political, or organisational affiliations that could pose a conflict with the goals of the UNFCCC or the Paris Agreement.
Clearly identify all individuals seconded, contracted, or appointed to advisory or consultative roles, and
• disclose any relevant interests.

• Ensure that the Presidency team and national delegation do not include representatives of fossil fuel or other high-polluting industries. Publicly encourage other State Parties to apply similar integrity standards when composing their national delegations, while respecting their sovereign discretion.
Open lobbying register and transparency
Commit to making a draft Host Country Agreement (HCA) publicly available prior to signature to enable
• feedback from observers and civil society. Promptly publish the final HCA online following signature, in line with the June 2023 Subsidiary Body for Implementation guidance.
Publish details of any consultancies or contracts with third parties linked to the delivery of COP31, their
• scope and financial implications, and adhere to UNFCCC Secretariat’s own guidelines on partnerships with entities linked to the fossil fuel industry or other high‑polluting sectors21.
Establish and maintain a public lobbying register documenting all meetings between the Presidency and

• external stakeholders, including industry representatives, lobbyists, and consulting firms, throughout COP planning and implementation. Ensure the register records: organisations met, topics discussed, summaries of outcomes, and dates.
Independent oversight and advisory mechanisms
• Appoint an independent ethics adviser or panel to oversee implementation of integrity measures, provide
guidance, and act on transparency and accountability concerns.
Conflict of interest safeguards
Adopt and implement internal conflict‑of‑interest procedures covering real and perceived conflicts,
including rules on gifts, outside employment, and post-tenure employment (“revolving door” risks).
Make these safeguards publicly available and integrate them into staff onboarding.
• Ensure conflict-of-interest policies explicitly treat affiliations with fossil fuel and other high-polluting
industries as incompatible with the responsibilities of the COP Presidency and the objectives of the Paris
Agreement and UNFCCC.
